label: 2 Timothy 1:3–7
text:
Paul's 'I thank God' is present tense — an ongoing habit of gratitude, not a single act.

'Serve' translates latreuō, the word for the priest's sacred duty at the altar; Paul frames his whole life, inherited from his forebears, as an act of worship.

'I am reminded' renders hupomnēsis, recollection triggered by an outside prompt rather than anamnēsis, memory that simply surfaces on its own — something jogged Paul's memory of Timothy's tears.

'Unfeigned' is anupokritos, built from the same root that gives us 'hypocrite,' the word for a Greek stage actor performing behind a mask; the negating alpha in front describes faith with no mask at all, no performance.

'Dwelt in' is enoikeō, 'to live at home in' — the faith that first lived in Lois and Eunice has settled residence in Timothy too.

'Stir up' is anazōpureō, literally 'kindle the fire again,' built from words for 'again,' 'life,' and 'fire' — and it's a present-tense infinitive, so the command isn't to strike one spark but to keep tending the flame continuously.

The 'gift' is a charisma, Spirit-given, bundled with 'power, love, and a sound mind' set directly against deilia, cowardly timidity — the very opposite of what God handed Timothy.
translation: I am continually thankful to God, whom I continually serve as my forefathers did, with a clean conscience, as I hold you unceasingly in my petitions, yearning night and day to see you, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy — having been reminded of the unmasked faith that is in you, which was at home first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and, I am persuaded, is at home in you also. For this reason I am reminding you: keep on fanning into flame the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but of power and love and a sound mind.

label: 2 Timothy 1:8
text:
'Be not ashamed' uses the aorist subjunctive with the negative, not the present imperative — the grammar forbids an action not yet begun rather than commanding Timothy to stop something already underway. Paul isn't rebuking existing shame; he's heading off a temptation that hasn't yet taken hold.

'His prisoner' doesn't mean a man Christ has locked up, but a man who belongs to Christ and wears chains for that reason — the genitive marks possession, not agency.

'Be partaker of the afflictions' translates sugkakopatheō, a compound stacking 'with' onto 'suffer' onto 'evil' — literally, to suffer hardship together with someone. Timothy isn't asked to suffer alone; he's asked to share Paul's and the Lord's own sufferings.

And the strength for that sharing is qualified — 'according to the power of God' — so the endurance asked of him is never presented as self-generated grit.
translation: Therefore, do not begin to be ashamed of the testimony that belongs to our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner — but suffer hardship together with us for the sake of the gospel, according to the power of God.

label: 2 Timothy 1:9
text:
'Who saved' pins the verb to a specific historical moment — an aorist participle, not an ongoing process — because Paul's argument is that a settled, one-time act of God back then guarantees his continued power now.

Salvation is 'not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace': kata carries the sense of 'down,' of domination or control, so Paul is saying our works exercise no control whatsoever over how salvation is given.

That grace, he adds, was granted 'before eternal times' — a phrase reaching back of any reckoned time at all, lodged in God's purpose before creation existed to receive it.

Then, moving into the next two verses, 'made manifest' (phaneroō) means bringing into visibility something that had been hidden; 'appearing' is epiphaneia, the word Greek writers used for a god's glorious self-disclosure, here applied to Christ's incarnation.

'Abolished' translates katargeō, 'rendered inoperative' — not erased, since believers still die, but stripped of its power to terrify or hold.

Paul calls himself a kērux, 'herald' — the term for the Emperor's own officer, who proclaimed the sovereign's message with a formality and authority that demanded a hearing.
translation: The One who saved us — at that decisive moment — and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before times eternal, but has now been made visible through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who rendered death inoperative and brought life and incorruption to light through the gospel — the gospel for which I was appointed a herald, an ambassador, and a teacher.

label: 2 Timothy 1:12
text:
'I know' is oida, not ginōskō — not knowledge gained through experience but flat, settled certainty about who God is.

Both 'I have believed' and 'am persuaded' sit in the perfect tense: not 'I believed once' but 'I came to believe, and that belief still stands, fixed.'

'Able' is dunatos, a word that carries more than bare capability — it points to power actually resident in the one described.

'Keep' is phulassō, a soldier's term for standing guard.

What's guarded — 'that which I have committed to him' — reads best in context as the deposit of gospel truth entrusted to Paul's care as herald and teacher, not his own soul's safekeeping; the surrounding verses are all about service, not salvation.

'That day' points ahead to the reckoning where that stewardship gets evaluated.
translation: For this reason I am also suffering these things. But I am not ashamed, for I know — with absolute certainty — the One in whom I have placed my trust, and I have come to a settled persuasion that he is powerful enough to guard, until that day, what has been entrusted to me.

label: 2 Timothy 1:13
text:
'Pattern' is hupotupōsis, built on tupos, the word for the mark a stamp or seal leaves behind — an impression that reproduces the original exactly. Paul isn't asking Timothy to preserve a vague memory of the gospel's gist; he's asking him to keep the precise wording he was taught, the way a die keeps the shape it was cut to. The phrase matters for how the New Testament regards its own words — not just its ideas, but its actual vocabulary, treated as worth guarding letter for letter.

'In faith and love' names the spirit in which that guarding is to be done — not rigid formalism, but conviction wrapped in warmth.
translation: Keep holding fast the pattern of sound words which you heard from me personally, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

label: 2 Timothy 1:14
text:
'That good thing committed to you' is literally 'the beautiful deposit' — Paul keeps returning to deposit-language for the gospel entrusted to Timothy, treating doctrine like something banked, to be guarded rather than improved on.

'Keep' again is phulassō, standing guard.

And the guarding isn't a solo effort — it happens 'through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us,' enoikeō, the same 'at home' word used earlier of Timothy's faith. The Spirit isn't a visitor lodging temporarily; he's meant to be fully at home, free to do his sanctifying work without resistance.
translation: That beautiful trust which was deposited with you, guard through the Holy Spirit who is at home in us.

label: 2 Timothy 1:15
text:
'Asia' here is the Roman province in western Asia Minor, not a continent — a compact region, which makes the scope of the defection sharper: a whole province's believers turning from Paul. The turning wasn't personal pique; the same two names, Phygellus and Hermogenes, resurface later tied to doctrinal error, so this was a theological break, not a falling-out. Then, moving into the next two verses, Onesiphorus stands in deliberate contrast.

'Refreshed' is anapsuchō, 'to cool off' — a vivid, almost physical word for the relief he brought Paul.

'Chain' is halusis, a manacle; Paul was literally handcuffed to a Roman guard around the clock, and visiting him carried real risk.

'Very diligently' uses a comparative form — Onesiphorus searched with more effort than anyone could reasonably have expected.
translation: You know this — that all those in Asia turned away from me, among them Phygellus and Hermogenes. May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often cooled my spirit and was not ashamed of my chain, but when he arrived in Rome he kept seeking me out with more-than-expected diligence, and found me.

label: 2 Timothy 1:18
text:
'Better' is a comparative — Timothy, as Ephesus's own pastor, actually knew more about Onesiphorus's service there than Paul did; a small, human touch.

Chapter two opens with the pronoun 'you' placed for emphasis — 'as for you' — as Paul turns urgently from his own situation to Timothy's future conduct.

'Be strong' is endunamoō, a passive form: Timothy isn't told to grit his teeth but to be strengthened, the power coming from outside him, 'in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.'

'Commit' is paratithēmi, the deposit-word again — Timothy is to bank the gospel with men whose defining trait is pistos, not 'believing' so much as 'trustworthy,' reliable enough to be handed something valuable.

The soldier image that follows sharpens the point: 'endure hardship' is sunkakopatheō, built with the same 'with' prefix as in 1:8 — Timothy suffers hardship alongside Paul, not alone.

A soldier on campaign doesn't get 'entangled' (emplekō, literally 'inwoven') in civilian business, because his whole purpose is to satisfy the one who enlisted him. The image trades on the plain fact that a man can't serve two masters with divided attention.
translation: And how much he served me in Ephesus, you know better than I do. You, then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and the things you heard from me personally, in the presence of many witnesses, deposit as a trust with trustworthy men, men who will be sufficient to teach others also. Take your share in enduring hardship together with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier gets himself entangled in civilian affairs, so that he may please the one who enlisted him.

label: 2 Timothy 2:5
text:
'Strive for the mastery' is athleō, the verb behind our word 'athlete' — the term for competing in the public games.

Greek contestants underwent months of mandated training beforehand, under strict diet and discipline, before they were even allowed to compete; break the rules and you were disqualified — adokimos, 'failing the test,' the same word Paul uses of himself elsewhere. Paul's point rides on that detail: the wreath doesn't go to whoever crosses the line first, but to whoever competed inside the rules the whole way through.
translation: And if anyone competes as an athlete, he is not crowned unless he has competed according to the rules.

label: 2 Timothy 2:6
text:
'Husbandman' is geōrgos, a plain tiller of the soil, and 'laboureth' is kopiaō, work pushed to the point of exhaustion — not light effort but wearing toil.

'Must' is dei, 'it is necessary in the nature of the case' — not a suggestion but a built-in principle: the one who does the exhausting work has the first claim on what it produces. Paul is laying groundwork for the plain fact that gospel labor, done with that kind of effort, rightly supports the laborer.
translation: It is necessary, in the nature of the case, that the farmer who toils to the point of exhaustion be the first to share in the crops.

label: 2 Timothy 2:7
text: 'Consider' is noeō, 'grasp with the mind' — Paul isn't asking Timothy to file away three pleasant pictures but to work out what each one demands of him: the soldier's undivided focus, the athlete's disciplined obedience to the rules, the farmer's willingness to labor hard before he can expect a return.
translation: Grasp the meaning of what I am saying; for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.

label: 2 Timothy 2:8–10
text:
'Raised from the dead' is a perfect participle — not simply 'he rose' but 'he was raised, and remains, permanently, alive.'

'From the dead' is literally 'out from among the dead ones': Christ rose out of that company while the rest stayed in it, which is exactly why his resurrection functions as the guarantee, not just an example, of ours.

'Evildoer' is kakourgos, a technical legal term for a criminal — the specific charge under which Paul was chained, 'to the extent of bonds.'

But 'the word of God is not bound' uses the perfect tense too: it 'has not been shackled, and remains unshackled' — Paul's imprisonment can restrain his body but not the message.

'The elect' comes from eklegō, 'to pick out'; those picked out are chosen not merely for their own benefit but with a view to the salvation of others through them, which is why Paul can call his own suffering something endured for their sake.
translation: Keep remembering Jesus Christ, raised out from among the dead, from the offspring of David, according to my gospel, for which I am suffering hardship to the point of chains, as a criminal. But the word of God has not been shackled — it remains unshackled. For this reason I am enduring all things for the sake of the chosen ones, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, together with eternal glory.

label: 2 Timothy 2:11–13
text:
'If' throughout this saying is the particle for a fulfilled condition — not a hypothetical 'suppose we died with him' but 'since we did die with him,' an aorist pointing to an accomplished fact, the believer's identification with Christ's death and resurrection.

'We shall live with him' pairs 'with' with the instrumental case — life not merely alongside Christ but by means of him, he himself being the life.

'Believe not' doesn't describe honest doubt; in this context it means unfaithfulness — proving untrue to him in how one actually lives, not failing to intellectually assent. And the last line turns on God's own nature rather than ours: he remains faithful because faithfulness is what he is — for him to abandon that would be to deny himself, which his own character rules out.
translation: Trustworthy is this statement: since we died together with him, we shall also live by means of him; since we are enduring, we shall also reign as kings with him; since we are denying him, that One will deny us; since we are being unfaithful, that One remains faithful — for he is not able to deny himself.

label: 2 Timothy 2:14
text:
'Strive about words' is logomacheō, a compound built straight from 'word' and 'fight' — literally 'word-fighting,' wrangling over phrasing rather than substance.

Paul says it produces nothing chrēsimos, 'fit for use' — not that it's merely unhelpful, but that it yields nothing usable at all.

'Subverting' is katastrephō, the root of our word 'catastrophe' — the picture is of ground plowed under or a city leveled, not a minor setback but a ruin.
translation: Keep reminding them of these things, solemnly charging them before God not to be endlessly word-fighting — a practice that produces not one useful thing, but ruins those who listen.

label: 2 Timothy 2:15
text:
'Study' is spoudazō, a verb of urgency — 'make haste, exert full effort,' not leisurely diligence but hustle.

'Shew thyself approved' pairs paristēmi, 'present, exhibit,' with dokimos, the word for something tested and found up to standard — Paul pictures a workman whose work has passed inspection, with nothing to be ashamed of when it's examined.

'Rightly dividing' is orthotomeō, 'cut straight' — a compound that suggests the careful, exact work of a mason squaring stone or a craftsman cutting cloth true to the line, applied here to handling the truth honestly rather than twisting it to score points.

Paul then turns to what to avoid: 'shun' is periistēmi, 'turn yourself around and away from' — an active sidestep, not passive avoidance.

'Profane' is bebēlos, built from the word for a threshold anyone may tread — common ground, as opposed to what is set apart.

'Vain babblings' is kenophōnia, 'empty sound' — and Paul's point is that emptiness never stays empty; since nature won't tolerate a vacuum, hollow talk fills itself with something, and that something is corruption.

'Canker' is gangraina, our own word gangrene — the picture of infection that, left untreated, keeps spreading and eating away at healthy tissue, exactly what false teaching does to a church body.
translation: Make every effort to present yourself to God approved — a workman with nothing to be ashamed of, cutting a straight path through the word of truth. But turn yourself away from unhallowed, empty talk — for it will progress further into ungodliness, and their word will spread like gangrene.

label: 2 Timothy 2:19
text:
'The foundation of God standeth sure' actually reads 'the firm foundation of God stands' — 'firm,' meaning immovable, modifies foundation directly rather than asserting its stability as a separate claim.

'Standeth' is a perfect tense: it has stood, and by virtue of that, stands now, permanently. The seal that follows carries two inscriptions functioning as one unit — one describing God's own certain knowledge of who belongs to him, the other calling those who claim that name to a matching holiness.

'Nameth' is onomazō, not casual reference but a pronouncing of the name as a claim — invoking it is itself a confession of allegiance, and Paul ties that confession directly to an obligation: depart from unrighteousness or the naming is empty.
translation: Nevertheless, God's firm foundation has stood, and stands now, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his, and, Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness.

label: 2 Timothy 2:22
text:
'Flee' and 'follow' are set as opposites in force: 'follow' is diōkō, 'pursue' — the same word Paul uses elsewhere for chasing down a goal with real exertion, not casual imitation.

'Faith' here is better read as 'faithfulness,' in the sense of fidelity and reliability, since Paul is listing virtues rather than talking about belief.

'Charity' is agapē — not almsgiving, as the English word suggests today, but the deliberate, self-giving love the Spirit produces, the kind willing to spend itself for someone else's good.
translation: Keep fleeing the passions of youth, but keep pursuing righteousness, faithfulness, love, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord out of a clean heart.

label: 2 Timothy 2:23
text:
'Unlearned' is apaideutos — the negative of the verb 'to train a child' — describing not a lack of book-knowledge but a mind that's never been disciplined, never drilled in how to think.

'Avoid' is a flat refusal, and 'gender' is 'beget' — Paul pictures these undisciplined questions as literally fathering quarrels, a natural offspring rather than an occasional side effect.
translation: But refuse foolish and undisciplined questionings, knowing that they constantly beget quarrels.

label: 2 Timothy 2:24–26
text:
'Servant' is doulos, 'bondslave' — the Lord's, and by extension his people's, complete possession.

'Gentle' describes outward demeanor rather than inner disposition, and 'instructing' is better rendered 'correcting,' since the verb here carries the sense of setting someone straight rather than merely informing them.

The verb 'will give' is optative — a mood marking an outcome as undetermined, a remote possibility rather than a guarantee, which fits Paul's carefully tentative 'if perhaps.'

'Recover themselves' is literally 'sober up' — the same image used elsewhere for waking from a drunken stupor, matched against 'taken captive,' a perfect participle describing people who have been and remain held by the devil's snare. Correction, on this picture, isn't punishing an enemy; it's trying to rouse someone out of an intoxication they didn't fully choose.
translation: And the Lord's bondslave must not, in the nature of the case, quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, skilled in teaching, patient of wrongs, correcting his opponents with gentleness — perhaps God may grant them repentance leading to a precise knowledge of the truth, and they may sober up out of the devil's snare, where they have been held captive, to do that One's will.

label: 2 Timothy 3:8
text:
'Withstood' is anistēmi, 'to set oneself against' — deliberate, active opposition, not passive disagreement. Paul draws the comparison in degree, not method: these teachers oppose the truth the way Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses — not necessarily by magic, but with the same stubborn intensity.

'Reprobate' is adokimos, the same word used elsewhere for failing a test — men who have been examined and found wanting, disqualified with respect to the very faith they claim to teach.
translation: Now, just as Jannes and Jambres set themselves against Moses, so these also set themselves against the truth — men corrupted in mind, disqualified concerning the faith, having been tested and found wanting.

label: 2 Timothy 3:9
text:
'Proceed' is prokoptō, literally 'hammer forward' — the picture of a smith forging metal by repeated blows, here used of advancing in a course of action.

Paul says that forward motion will stop; their anoia, 'folly' — a word carrying overtones of derangement, not mere mistake — will become as publicly obvious as it did with Jannes and Jambres, whose tricks collapsed in front of Pharaoh's court.
translation: But they will make no further progress, for their derangement will become obvious to everyone, just as that of those two became obvious.

label: 2 Timothy 3:10–11
text:
'Hast fully known' is parakoloutheō, a compound meaning literally 'to follow alongside' — the word for a disciple who attaches himself to a teacher and stays close, conforming his own life to the pattern.

It's stronger than 'you learned facts about me'; it describes discipleship, the aorist tense pointing back to the specific moment Timothy threw in his lot with Paul.

The pronoun 'you' is placed for emphasis — 'you, in contrast to others' — as Paul singles Timothy out from those in Asia who had turned away.
translation: But as for you, you attached yourself as a disciple to me — because of my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, the persecutions and sufferings that happened to me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, such persecutions as I endured; and out of them all the Lord rescued me.

label: 2 Timothy 3:12
text: 'Will live godly' isn't a flat future tense — the verb is thelō, 'to desire, to be bent on.' Paul isn't predicting that godly living happens to attract persecution; he's saying that anyone whose will is actually set on a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, as a matter of course, not as an unlucky exception.
translation: And all, in fact, who are determined to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.

label: 2 Timothy 3:13
text:
'Seducers' is goēs, originally the word for a wailing incantation-chanter — a sorcerer who works by spells — narrowed here to mean an outright impostor.

'Wax worse and worse' is prokoptō again, the same 'hammer forward' word from the previous verse — these men make progress too, but in the wrong direction, deceiving others while sliding further into their own self-deception, the same verb working both ways at once.
translation: But pernicious men and impostors will progress further toward the worst, deceiving and being deceived.

label: 2 Timothy 4:2
text:
'Preach' is kērussō, the verb for a herald's formal proclamation of an emperor's message — delivered with an authority that expects to be heeded, not a speaker's private opinion offered for consideration. The command form itself is sharp and summary, almost military.

'Be instant in season, out of season' uses a word meaning 'stand ready, be at hand' — Timothy is to hold himself in constant readiness whether the moment is favorable or unfavorable; there's no closed season on the task. Two different words for correction follow.

'Reprove' is elegchō, a rebuke aimed at bringing the hearer to actually acknowledge guilt.

'Rebuke' is epitimaō, sharper and more severe, used whether or not the person ever admits fault — it carries a hint of consequences to come.

'Exhort' softens the tone again: it means 'urge, plead, beg,' and it's to be done with makrothumia, a temper that absorbs provocation without lashing back, paired with solid teaching rather than mere emotional pressure.
translation: Herald the word with full authority. Stand ready with it whether the time is opportune or inopportune. Reprove so as to bring conviction; rebuke sharply; plead and urge — doing all this with a temper that will not retaliate, and with careful, patient instruction.

label: 2 Timothy 4:5
text:
'Watch' is nēphō, 'be sober, alert, clear-headed' — the opposite of drifting through the work in a fog.

'Endure hardships' is a sharp aorist imperative, a crisp command rather than a gentle suggestion — fitting, since Timothy's temperament tended toward caution rather than grit.

'Evangelist' has no definite article in the Greek, which shifts the weight from office to character: not 'go take up the office of evangelist' but 'let your work carry an evangelistic quality' — every pastor's ministry should have that outward reach built in.

'Make full proof' means 'carry a thing through to completion, perform it fully' — nothing done by halves.
translation: But as for you, be sober-minded in all things, endure hardship, let your work carry the character of one who brings good news, and carry your ministry through to its full completion.

label: 2 Timothy 4:6
text:
'I am now ready to be offered' uses spendomai, the word for a drink-offering poured out at a pagan altar — the same image Paul reaches for in Philippians, of his own blood as a libation poured over the more important sacrifice, the church's service.

'Departure' is analuō, literally 'to unloose, break up' — a word soldiers used for striking camp and sailors used for weighing anchor. Paul the tentmaker reaches for the soldier's picture: he's not ending, he's breaking camp.

'Is at hand' means 'stands ready, present' — as though death itself were already standing at the tent flap.
translation: For as for me, my blood is already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time for me to break camp has arrived.

label: 2 Timothy 4:7
text:
All three verbs here sit in the perfect tense — not 'I fought, ran, kept' as isolated past events, but 'I have fought, and the fight is settled; I have run, and the race is over; I have guarded, and the trust stands secure' — completed action with a present, ongoing result.

'The good fight' carries the definite article in Greek, 'the fight,' the specific one set before him, not a generic contest; and 'good' here points to external, visible beauty of execution rather than moral goodness — the aesthetics of a fight well fought, the way a wrestler's form can be called beautiful.

'Course' is a runner's track.

'Kept' is 'guard' — the same stewardship language Paul has used throughout the letter for the gospel deposit.
translation: I have fought the good fight to its finish, and I am resting now in its victory. I have run the course to its end, and I am resting now at the finish line. I have guarded the trust, and it stands secure.

label: 2 Timothy 4:8
text:
'Crown' is stephanos, the athlete's victory wreath, not a royal diadem — Paul is still standing at the finish line from the previous verse, now looking toward the awards stand.

'Judge' is kritēs, which in this athletic picture reads as 'umpire,' the official who scores the contest fairly, not a courtroom figure.

'Give' means 'award' — the vocabulary of handing out a prize that's been earned within the rules.

'Loved his appearing' uses a perfect-tense verb: a love that was fixed on Christ's return at some point and has stayed fixed there ever since, a settled orientation of life rather than a passing sentiment.
translation: From now on, there is reserved for me the victor's wreath of righteousness, which the Lord, the umpire who judges rightly, will award me on that day — and not only to me, but to all who have set their love, and kept it set, on his appearing.

label: 2 Timothy 4:9
text: 'Do thy diligence' is spoudazō again, the same urgent 'make every effort' verb Paul used earlier in this letter — this isn't a casual invitation but a request pressed with real urgency. Paul is alone and running out of time.
translation: Make every effort to come to me quickly.

label: 2 Timothy 4:10–12
text:
'Forsaken' is egkataleipō, a compound built from 'leave,' 'down,' and 'in' — stronger than plain desertion, it pictures leaving someone down in circumstances stacked against him, helpless.

It's the same verb behind our expression 'let down.'

'World' is aiōn, not the physical earth but the present age — its whole climate of values, the pull Demas apparently found more attractive than standing by a chained old man.

A small grammatical hinge matters in verse 12: the connecting word is adversative, 'but,' distinguishing Tychicus, whom Paul himself dispatched to Ephesus, from Crescens and Titus, who had left on their own initiative.

'Take Mark' means literally 'pick up' — a practical, en-route instruction, not a formal summons.
translation: For Demas let me down — he set his heart on this present age and came to love it — and he went off to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Pick up Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for the work. But Tychicus I sent off to Ephesus.

label: 2 Timothy 4:13
text:
'Cloak' names a specific garment — a circular, felt travel-cape reaching to the knees, the kind woven from the same tough goat's hair Paul had handled for years as a tentmaker, made to shed wind and rain.

'Books' are papyrus rolls; 'parchments' are animal-skin manuscripts, more durable and valuable than papyrus. Even facing execution, Paul is still asking for his library.

In the verses that follow about Alexander, 'did me much evil' points to actual deeds, not just words.

'The Lord will reward him' is a plain future tense, a statement of fact rather than a curse invoked in anger.

'Beware' turns the guarding word toward self-protection — a term that assumes the threat comes from outside, an assault to be defended against rather than provoked.
translation: Bring, when you come, the cloak I left at Troas with Carpus, and the papyrus rolls — above all, the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will pay him back according to his deeds. Be on guard against him yourself, for he strongly opposed our words.

label: 2 Timothy 4:16
text:
'Answer' is apologia, literally 'a talking of oneself off from' a charge — the technical term for a formal legal defense.

'No man stood with me' uses the word for someone appearing in court on the accused's behalf, as advocate or character witness. Nobody showed up.

'Forsook' is the same word used of Demas earlier in the chapter — the whole church in Rome, in that moment, let him down.
translation: At my first defense, no one stood at my side — everyone let me down. May it not be counted against them.

label: 2 Timothy 4:17
text:
Where no human advocate appeared, 'the Lord stood with me' uses a verb meaning 'stand alongside' — the same one Paul uses elsewhere for standing by someone and taking responsibility for their needs. The Lord filled the role no one else would.

'Strengthened' pictures being clothed with strength from outside, not summoning it from within.

'Delivered out of the mouth of the lion' echoes the language of the Psalms — not a claim that Paul escaped execution, since he's already spoken of his blood being poured out, but that he wasn't defeated by fear into silence; he got to finish proclaiming the gospel before the whole imperial court.
translation: But the Lord stood at my side and clothed me with strength, so that through me the proclamation might be fully made and all the Gentiles might hear it. And I was pulled out of the lion's mouth.

label: 2 Timothy 4:18–22
text:
'Deliver' is ruomai, a tender word meaning 'to draw to oneself, out of harm's way' — rescue pictured as being pulled close rather than merely being spared.

And 'every evil work' most likely points inward rather than outward: not protection from some external villain, but from the one failure Paul would have counted truly evil — collapsing into silence instead of testifying when it mattered most. He closes with the ordinary business of any letter: greetings, news of where his coworkers are, a last request to come before winter.
translation: And the Lord will draw me to himself, away from every pernicious deed, and will keep me safe for his heavenly kingdom — to him be the glory forever and ever. Amen. Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained in Corinth, and Trophimus I left behind in Miletus, sick. Make every effort to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
